papers.research_question: What is the role of multi-head self-attention in supporting multilingual processing in LLMs? Specifically, are there language-specific and language-general attention heads, and how can they be used to control model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LAHIS, a method to identify language-specific and language-general attention heads in multilingual LLMs, and shows how modulating these heads can control cross-lingual attention and improve multilingual performance with minimal parameters.
papers.conclusion: The work enhances interpretability of multilingual behaviors in LLMs from the perspective of MHA and presents practical approaches to strengthen multilingual capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
LAHIS reveals the existence of language-specific and language-general attention heads in multilingual LLMs.
Language-specific heads enable cross-lingual attention transfer, allowing steering of model attention to target languages.
Modulating language-specific heads mitigates off-target language generation by suppressing English-heads.
A lightweight adaptation using a trainable matrix on language-specific heads improves multilingual question answering accuracy with only 14-20 parameters.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support multilingual understanding and generation. Meanwhile, efforts to interpret their internal mechanisms have emerged, offering insights to enhance multilingual performance. While multi-head self-attention (MHA) has proven critical in many areas, its role in multilingual capabilities remains underexplored. In this work, we study the contribution of MHA in supporting multilingual processing in LLMs. We propose Language Attention Head Importance Scores (LAHIS), an effective and efficient method that identifies attention head importance for multilingual capabilities via a single forward and backward pass through the LLM. Applying LAHIS to Aya-23-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Mistral-7B-v0.1, we reveal the existence of both language-specific and language-general heads. Language-specific heads enable cross-lingual attention transfer to guide the model toward target language contexts and mitigate off-target language generation issue, contributing to addressing challenges in multilingual LLMs. We also introduce a lightweight adaptation that learns a soft head mask to modulate attention outputs over language heads, requiring only 20 tunable parameters to improve XQuAD accuracy. Overall, our work enhances both the interpretability and multilingual capabilities of LLMs from the perspective of MHA.

papers.title: Language models align with brain regions that represent concepts across modalities
papers.research_question: Do language models align with brain regions that represent concepts consistently across different input modalities (text and images)?
papers.core_contribution: Language models predict brain activity better in regions with high semantic consistency across modalities, even when those regions are not language-selective, suggesting LMs develop cross-modal conceptual representations.
papers.conclusion: Language models align with brain regions that represent concepts consistently across modalities, indicating that LMs may internally develop cross-modal conceptual representations.
papers.key_findings:
Brain regions with higher semantic consistency (responding similarly to concepts across text and image paradigms) are better predicted by LM representations.
This correlation holds even in brain regions with weak language selectivity.
Representational similarity between LMs and semantically consistent brain regions is significant and increases for vision-language models when using both text and image stimuli.
Both language-only and vision-language models show alignment with semantically consistent brain regions.
papers.limitation:
The picture paradigm correlation is lower and skewed by visual cortex areas that encode images but not necessarily concepts.
The study uses an inter-participant noise ceiling due to lack of repeated trials, which may not capture all variability.
papers.abstract: Cognitive science and neuroscience have long faced the challenge of disentangling representations of language from representations of conceptual meaning. As the same problem arises in today's language models (LMs), we investigate the relationship between LM--brain alignment and two neural metrics: (1) the level of brain activation during processing of sentences, targeting linguistic processing, and (2) a novel measure of meaning consistency across input modalities, which quantifies how consistently a brain region responds to the same concept across paradigms (sentence, word cloud, image) using an fMRI dataset (Pereira et al., 2018). Our experiments show that both language-only and language-vision models predict the signal better in more meaning-consistent areas of the brain, even when these areas are not strongly sensitive to language processing, suggesting that LMs might internally represent cross-modal conceptual meaning.

papers.title: Cross-neutralising: Probing for joint encoding of linguistic information in multilingual models
papers.research_question: How are linguistic properties encoded jointly across typologically-similar languages in multilingual models like M-BERT and XLM-R?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that multilingual models jointly encode typological linguistic properties across languages, and this can be probed using the cross-neutralising method.
papers.conclusion: Typological feature values are encoded jointly across languages in multilingual models and can be localized via language centroids.
papers.key_findings:
Self-neutralising by subtracting language centroids removes typological information, reducing probing accuracy to chance levels.
Cross-neutralising shows that performance deteriorates for languages sharing the same typological feature value, indicating joint encoding.
This joint encoding pattern is observed in both M-BERT and XLM-R models.
The effect is consistent across different layers of the models.
Language centroids capture specific feature values in a localizable way across languages.
papers.limitation: When probing performance before neutralising is low (<75% accuracy), it is unclear what information the language centroids capture, limiting the interpretation of results.
future_direction: Correlate typological feature encoding with downstream task performance
Use cross-neutralising for selective generalization in models based on typology
Apply the method to other scenarios like multimodal models
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders are widely used to transfer NLP models across languages. The success of this transfer is, however, dependent on the model's ability to encode the patterns of cross-lingual similarity and variation. Yet, little is known as to how these models are able to do this. We propose a simple method to study how relationships between languages are encoded in two state-of-the-art multilingual models (i.e. M-BERT and XLM-R). The results provide insight into their information sharing mechanisms and suggest that linguistic properties are encoded jointly across typologically-similar languages in these models.

papers.title: Neuron-Level Knowledge Attribution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to identify important neurons for knowledge storage in large language models, and how to distinguish between 'value neurons' that directly contribute to predictions and 'query neurons' that activate them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a static method based on log probability increase to identify important 'value neurons' in LLMs, and a method based on inner products to identify 'query neurons' that activate them, showing superior performance compared to other static methods.
papers.conclusion: The study proposes a method based on log probability increase to identify important 'value neurons' and a method based on inner products to locate the 'query neurons' activating them, which aids in understanding the mechanism of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Both attention and FFN layers can store knowledge, and all important neurons directly contributing to knowledge prediction are in deep layers.
In attention layers, knowledge with similar semantics tends to be stored in the same heads, while distinct semantics are stored in different heads.
Intervening on a few value neurons (300) or query neurons (1000) can significantly influence the final prediction.
FFN value neurons are mainly activated by medium-deep attention value neurons, which are mainly activated by shallow/medium FFN query neurons.
The proposed attribution method outperforms seven other static methods across three metrics.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on six specific types of knowledge, while other types are also important.
Experiments are conducted only on GPT2-large and Llama-7B models; comparison across different models is needed.
Uses static methods for attribution and does not compare with other attribution methods like causal mediation analysis and gradient-based methods.
future_direction: Compare static methods with other attribution methods like causal mediation analysis and gradient-based methods.
Explore knowledge storage in other types of knowledge and across different models.
Improve attribution methods to better capture the importance of deepest layers and interpretability of query neurons.
papers.abstract: Identifying important neurons for final predictions is essential for understanding the mechanisms of large language models. Due to computational constraints, current attribution techniques struggle to operate at neuron level. In this paper, we propose a static method for pinpointing significant neurons. Compared to seven other methods, our approach demonstrates superior performance across three metrics. Additionally, since most static methods typically only identify "value neurons" directly contributing to the final prediction, we propose a method for identifying "query neurons" which activate these "value neurons". Finally, we apply our methods to analyze six types of knowledge across both attention and feed-forward network (FFN) layers. Our method and analysis are helpful for understanding the mechanisms of knowledge storage and set the stage for future research in knowledge editing. The code is available on https://github.com/zepingyu0512/neuron-attribution.

papers.title: How Training Data Shapes the Use of Parametric and In-Context Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: What training data properties enable language models to robustly utilize both parametric and in-context knowledge and resolve conflicts between them?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies three training data properties—intra-document repetition, within-document inconsistency, and skewed knowledge frequency distribution—that must co-occur for robust knowledge utilization and conflict resolution in language models.
papers.conclusion: The study provides the first systematic analysis showing that intra-document repetition, inconsistency, and skewed knowledge distribution are essential for robust knowledge utilization, offering practical guidance for training data design.
papers.key_findings:
Intra-document repetition enables the co-emergence of parametric and in-context knowledge utilization, with in-context knowledge utilization emerging first.
A moderate level of within-document inconsistency prevents over-reliance on in-context knowledge and induces a preference transition towards parametric knowledge as training progresses.
A skewed knowledge frequency distribution preserves in-context knowledge utilization capabilities by ensuring continuous usage for rare entities.
These properties jointly enable balanced reliance on both knowledge sources and confidence-dependent arbitration.
Instruction tuning can reshape knowledge arbitration strategies, increasing reliance on in-context knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study uses synthetic biography datasets which may not fully reflect natural language richness.
Focuses on knowledge conflicts based on internal confidence, leaving other retrieval-augmented generation scenarios for future work.
future_direction: Investigation of diverse retrieval-augmented generation scenarios such as retrieval errors, partial relevance, and multi-document conflicts.
papers.abstract: Large language models leverage not only parametric knowledge acquired during training but also in-context knowledge provided at inference time, despite the absence of explicit training objectives for using both sources. Prior work has further shown that when these knowledge sources conflict, models resolve the tension based on their internal confidence, preferring parametric knowledge for high-confidence facts while deferring to contextual information for less familiar ones. However, the training conditions that give rise to such knowledge utilization behaviors remain unclear. To address this gap, we conduct controlled experiments in which we train language models while systematically manipulating key properties of the training data. Our results reveal a counterintuitive finding: three properties commonly regarded as detrimental must co-occur for robust knowledge utilization and conflict resolution to emerge: (i) intra-document repetition of information, (ii) a moderate degree of within-document inconsistency, and (iii) a skewed knowledge frequency distribution. We further validate that the same training dynamics observed in our controlled setting also arise during real-world language model pretraining, and we analyze how post-training procedures can reshape models' knowledge preferences. Together, our findings provide concrete empirical guidance for training language models that harmoniously integrate parametric and in-context knowledge.

papers.title: Reason to Rote: Rethinking Memorization in Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize label noise, and why does such memorization not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Memorization of noisy labels in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, with memories stored via distributed encoding and outlier heuristics in neurons.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that memorization of label noise builds on existing reasoning mechanisms, using distributed encoding and outlier heuristics, explaining the phenomenon of benign memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Models first learn to generalize on noisy training instances (predicting correct labels) before memorizing the noisy labels.
Even when producing memorized noisy labels, models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs corresponding to the correct labels.
Memorization and generalization circuits substantially overlap, indicating memorization builds on existing generalization mechanisms.
Memorization uses distributed encoding across multiple input tokens and intermediate results rather than a simple lookup.
In the FDA task, memorization occurs via 'outlier heuristics' where higher-layer MLP neurons slightly shift their activation patterns to fit noisy labels.
papers.limitation:
Focus on relatively small language models; larger models might exhibit different behaviors.
Models trained from scratch, so influence of pretraining data is not considered.
Examination of implicit reasoning without explicit solution steps; not studying models with explicit chain-of-thought.
future_direction: Study memorization in larger models
Investigate effect of pretraining on memorization and reasoning
Study memorization in models with explicit chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models readily memorize arbitrary training instances, such as label noise, yet they perform strikingly well on reasoning tasks. In this work, we investigate how language models memorize label noise, and why such memorization in many cases does not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities. Using two controllable synthetic reasoning datasets with noisy labels, four-digit addition (FDA) and two-hop relational reasoning (THR), we discover a reliance of memorization on generalizable reasoning mechanisms: models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs even when retrieving memorized noisy labels, and intervening reasoning adversely affects memorization. We further show that memorization operates through distributed encoding, i.e., aggregating various inputs and intermediate results, rather than building a look-up mechanism from inputs to noisy labels. Moreover, our FDA case study reveals memorization occurs via outlier heuristics, where existing neuron activation patterns are slightly shifted to fit noisy labels. Together, our findings suggest that memorization of label noise in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, shedding lights on the intriguing phenomenon of benign memorization.

papers.title: InversionView: A General-Purpose Method for Reading Information from Neural Activations
papers.research_question: How can we decipher the information encoded in neural activations? The paper proposes InversionView, a method to sample from the preimage of an activation to uncover the information content.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces InversionView, a method that samples from the preimage of an activation via a conditional decoder to uncover the information encoded in neural activations and understand model algorithms.
papers.conclusion: InversionView is a general-purpose method that effectively deciphers information in neural activations, enabling better understanding of model algorithms and simplifying interpretability workflows.
papers.key_findings:
InversionView can reveal both basic and complex information in activations, such as token counts and relative positions.
InversionView simplifies interpretability workflows, agreeing with prior circuit findings in GPT-2 small.
InversionView enabled the first fully verified circuit for a 3-digit addition model.
InversionView scales to larger models like GPT-2 for factual recall.
papers.limitation:
Training a decoder requires a dataset of activations and can be computationally expensive.
The decoder may not perfectly capture the preimage, leading to potential biases in the generated samples.
The method is currently limited to discrete sequences (text).
future_direction: Extend InversionView to continuous domains.
Improve decoder efficiency.
Automate interpretation using LLMs.
papers.abstract: The inner workings of neural networks can be better understood if we can fully decipher the information encoded in neural activations. In this paper, we argue that this information is embodied by the subset of inputs that give rise to similar activations. We propose InversionView, which allows us to practically inspect this subset by sampling from a trained decoder model conditioned on activations. This helps uncover the information content of activation vectors, and facilitates understanding of the algorithms implemented by transformer models. We present four case studies where we investigate models ranging from small transformers to GPT-2. In these studies, we show that InversionView can reveal clear information contained in activations, including basic information about tokens appearing in the context, as well as more complex information, such as the count of certain tokens, their relative positions, and abstract knowledge about the subject. We also provide causally verified circuits to confirm the decoded information.

papers.title: IRCAN: Mitigating Knowledge Conflicts in LLM Generation via Identifying and Reweighting Context-Aware Neurons
papers.research_question: How can knowledge conflicts in LLM generation be mitigated by identifying and reweighting neurons that are crucial for processing contextual cues?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes IRCAN, a framework that identifies context-aware neurons in LLMs using integrated gradients and enhances them via reweighting to mitigate knowledge conflicts by improving fidelity to contextual knowledge.
papers.conclusion: IRCAN effectively mitigates knowledge conflicts in LLMs by identifying and enhancing context-aware neurons, leading to more context-faithful generation across diverse models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
IRCAN significantly improves accuracy on knowledge conflict tasks, achieving gains of 129% for LLaMA-2-7B and 136% for LLaMA-3-8B on the MemoTrap dataset.
Ablation studies show that erasing the identified context-aware neurons causes a substantial drop in accuracy, while manipulating random neurons has little effect, validating their importance.
IRCAN can be seamlessly combined with context-aware decoding (CAD) to achieve further performance improvements.
The method is plug-and-play and effective across a variety of model families and scales without requiring fine-tuning.
The identified neurons are shared across data instances, indicating a general mechanism for context processing.
papers.limitation:
The context in the COSE_KRE and ECARE_KRE datasets is generated by ChatGPT and may contain inaccuracies, which can hinder precise neuron identification and enhancement.
The method requires a validation set to select hyperparameters (number of neurons to enhance and enhancement strength).
future_direction: Extending the method to other model families and a broader range of tasks.
Exploring dynamic selection of context-aware neurons on a per-instance basis.
papers.abstract: It is widely acknowledged that large language models (LLMs) encode a vast reservoir of knowledge after being trained on mass data. Recent studies disclose knowledge conflicts in LLM generation, wherein outdated or incorrect parametric knowledge (i.e., encoded knowledge) contradicts new knowledge provided in the context. To mitigate such knowledge conflicts, we propose a novel framework, IRCAN (Identifying and Reweighting Context-Aware Neurons) to capitalize on neurons that are crucial in processing contextual cues. Specifically, IRCAN first identifies neurons that significantly contribute to context processing, utilizing a context-aware attribution score derived from integrated gradients. Subsequently, the identified context-aware neurons are strengthened via reweighting. In doing so, we steer LLMs to generate context-sensitive outputs with respect to the new knowledge provided in the context. Extensive experiments conducted across a variety of models and tasks demonstrate that IRCAN not only achieves remarkable improvements in handling knowledge conflicts but also offers a scalable, plug-and-play solution that can be integrated seamlessly with existing models. Our codes are released at https://github.com/danshi777/IRCAN.

papers.title: Grokked Transformers are Implicit Reasoners: A Mechanistic Journey to the Edge of Generalization
papers.research_question: Can transformers learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge, and how does grokking enable this? What are the differences in systematic generalization between composition and comparison tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge through grokking, but systematic generalization varies: composition fails out-of-distribution while comparison succeeds. Mechanistic analysis reveals the formation of generalizing circuits and explains the differences, guiding data and training setups and suggesting architectural improvements.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are capable of learning implicit reasoning through grokking, but the level of systematic generalization depends on the task and the circuit configuration. The findings guide data and training setups and suggest improvements to the transformer architecture for better cross-layer memory sharing.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can learn implicit reasoning only through grokking (extended training far beyond overfitting).
The speed of grokking correlates with the ratio of inferred to atomic facts (data distribution), not the absolute training data size.
For composition, transformers fail to generalize systematically to out-of-distribution examples, while for comparison, they succeed.
Mechanistic analysis reveals distinct generalizing circuits: for composition, a sequential circuit that stores atomic facts in separate layers; for comparison, a parallel circuit that stores atomic facts in the same layer.
In a complex reasoning task with a large search space, a fully grokked transformer achieves near-perfect accuracy, while state-of-the-art LLMs with non-parametric memory (GPT-4-Turbo, Gemini-1.5-Pro) fail regardless of prompting or retrieval augmentation.
papers.limitation:
The task formulation (induction and application of inference rules from atomic and inferred facts) may not apply to the full spectrum of reasoning types.
The study is limited to synthetic tasks and may not fully capture real-world reasoning complexities.
future_direction: Developing cross-layer memory-sharing mechanisms for transformers (e.g., memory-augmentation, explicit recurrence) to improve systematic generalization.
Investigating the tradeoff between parametric and non-parametric memory in language models.
Understanding the role of verbalizations (e.g., chain-of-thought) in teaching models to reason implicitly.
papers.abstract: We study whether transformers can learn to implicitly reason over parametric knowledge, a skill that even the most capable language models struggle with. Focusing on two representative reasoning types, composition and comparison, we consistently find that transformers can learn implicit reasoning, but only through grokking, i.e., extended training far beyond overfitting. The levels of generalization also vary across reasoning types: when faced with out-of-distribution examples, transformers fail to systematically generalize for composition but succeed for comparison. We delve into the model's internals throughout training, conducting analytical experiments that reveal: 1) the mechanism behind grokking, such as the formation of the generalizing circuit and its relation to the relative efficiency of generalizing and memorizing circuits, and 2) the connection between systematicity and the configuration of the generalizing circuit. Our findings guide data and training setup to better induce implicit reasoning and suggest potential improvements to the transformer architecture, such as encouraging cross-layer knowledge sharing. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for a challenging reasoning task with a large search space, GPT-4-Turbo and Gemini-1.5-Pro based on non-parametric memory fail badly regardless of prompting styles or retrieval augmentation, while a fully grokked transformer can achieve near-perfect accuracy, showcasing the power of parametric memory for complex reasoning.

papers.title: The Internal State of an LLM Knows When It's Lying
papers.research_question: Can the internal state of an LLM be used to reveal the truthfulness of statements, both provided to and generated by the LLM?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLM internal activations contain information about statement truthfulness and introduces SAPLMA, a classifier that uses these activations to detect false statements with higher accuracy than baselines like few-shot prompting.
papers.conclusion: SAPLMA leverages LLM hidden activations to predict statement truthfulness, offering a way to filter false information and increase trust in LLM-generated content.
papers.key_findings:
SAPLMA achieves accuracy between 60% to 80% on specific topics with OPT-6.7b and 70% to 90% with LLAMA2-7b, outperforming few-shot prompting which maxes at 56% accuracy.
The optimal hidden layer for SAPLMA varies between models, e.g., 20th layer for OPT-6.7b and middle layer for LLAMA2-7b.
Sentence probability assigned by the LLM is not a reliable indicator of truthfulness due to dependencies on sentence length and word frequencies.
SAPLMA can classify both externally provided statements and those generated by the LLM itself.
The method does not require fine-tuning the LLM, using only a trained classifier on frozen activations.
papers.limitation:
The method detects binary true/false, but in practice, detecting uncertainty or confidence levels might be more useful.
Tested only in English; applicability to multilingual settings is not verified.
For longer responses, activation values might need decoupling to isolate the most recent statement.
future_direction: Apply SAPLMA to larger LLMs and conduct human interaction experiments.
Study how activations develop over time as additional words are generated.
Extend to multilingual input and test cross-language applicability.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown exceptional performance in various tasks, one of their most prominent drawbacks is generating inaccurate or false information with a confident tone. In this paper, we provide evidence that the LLM's internal state can be used to reveal the truthfulness of statements. This includes both statements provided to the LLM, and statements that the LLM itself generates. Our approach is to train a classifier that outputs the probability that a statement is truthful, based on the hidden layer activations of the LLM as it reads or generates the statement. Experiments demonstrate that given a set of test sentences, of which half are true and half false, our trained classifier achieves an average of 71\% to 83\% accuracy labeling which sentences are true versus false, depending on the LLM base model. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between our classifier's performance and approaches based on the probability assigned to the sentence by the LLM. We show that while LLM-assigned sentence probability is related to sentence truthfulness, this probability is also dependent on sentence length and the frequencies of words in the sentence, resulting in our trained classifier providing a more reliable approach to detecting truthfulness, highlighting its potential to enhance the reliability of LLM-generated content and its practical applicability in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Promote, Suppress, Iterate: How Language Models Answer One-to-Many Factual Queries
papers.research_question: How do language models internally implement and integrate knowledge recall and repetition avoidance for one-to-many factual queries?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a promote-then-suppress mechanism in language models for one-to-many factual queries, where attention propagates subject information and MLPs promote answers, then attention suppresses previous answers with MLPs amplifying the suppression signal.
papers.conclusion: LMs promote all answers and then suppress previously generated ones, using attention and MLPs to integrate subject and previous answer tokens for knowledge recall and repetition avoidance.
papers.key_findings:
LMs first promote all possible answers and then suppress previously generated ones.
Attention copies subject information to the last token, and MLPs use this information to promote answers.
Previous answer tokens are used for both knowledge recall (promoting new answers) and suppression.
Attention suppresses previous answers, and MLPs amplify this suppression signal.
The last token aggregates knowledge recall and suppression information to generate distinct answers.
papers.limitation:
Low accuracy due to long-tail entities, outdated datasets, and strict exact-match evaluation.
Analysis focuses only on correct cases, not on errors or unreliable signals.
future_direction: Investigate possible redundancies in how LMs encode knowledge across multiple tokens.
Examine patterns when LMs use unreliable signals or make errors.
papers.abstract: To answer one-to-many factual queries (e.g., listing cities of a country), a language model (LM) must simultaneously recall knowledge and avoid repeating previous answers. How are these two subtasks implemented and integrated internally? Across multiple datasets, models, and prompt templates, we identify a promote-then-suppress mechanism: the model first recalls all answers, and then suppresses previously generated ones. Specifically, LMs use both the subject and previous answer tokens to perform knowledge recall, with attention propagating subject information and MLPs promoting the answers. Then, attention attends to and suppresses previous answer tokens, while MLPs amplify the suppression signal. Our mechanism is corroborated by extensive experimental evidence: in addition to using early decoding and causal tracing, we analyze how components use different tokens by introducing both Token Lens, which decodes aggregated attention updates from specified tokens, and a knockout method that analyzes changes in MLP outputs after removing attention to specified tokens. Overall, we provide new insights into how LMs' internal components interact with different input tokens to support complex factual recall. Code is available at https://github.com/Lorenayannnnn/how-lms-answer-one-to-many-factual-queries.

papers.title: Representational Stability of Truth in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How stable are LLM truth judgments under controlled semantic perturbations, and does internal representational stability predict behavioral stability? The paper investigates the role of epistemic familiarity in belief stability.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the P-StaT framework to evaluate belief stability in LLMs under semantic perturbations, and shows that epistemic familiarity (familiar vs. unfamiliar fictional content) governs stability in both representational and behavioral settings.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that epistemic familiarity is a robust signal for belief stability in LLMs, and that the P-StaT framework complements accuracy-based factuality evaluation with a notion of epistemic robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Unfamiliar Synthetic content induces the largest epistemic retractions in both representational and behavioral evaluations.
Familiar Fictional content is more representationally distinct and produces fewer retractions.
There is a decoupling between linguistic similarity and latent-space organization for Fictional content.
The stability hierarchy (Synthetic most destabilizing) is consistent across domains and LLMs.
Representational stability under probing perturbations predicts behavioral stability under zero-shot perturbations.
papers.limitation: Zero-shot retractions conflate belief changes with the number of baseline beliefs available to retract, making direct comparison with probing results difficult.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used for factual tasks such as "What treats asthma?" or "What is the capital of Latvia?". However, it remains unclear how stably LLMs encode distinctions between true, false, and neither-true-nor-false content in their internal probabilistic representations. We introduce representational stability as the robustness of an LLM's veracity representations to perturbations in the operational definition of truth. We assess representational stability by (i) training a linear probe on an LLM's activations to separate true from not-true statements and (ii) measuring how its learned decision boundary shifts under controlled label changes. Using activations from sixteen open-source models and three factual domains, we compare two types of neither statements. The first are fact-like assertions about entities we believe to be absent from any training data. We call these unfamiliar neither statements. The second are nonfactual claims drawn from well-known fictional contexts. We call these familiar neither statements. The unfamiliar statements induce the largest boundary shifts, producing up to $40\%$ flipped truth judgements in fragile domains (such as word definitions), while familiar fictional statements remain more coherently clustered and yield smaller changes ($\leq 8.2\%$). These results suggest that representational stability stems more from epistemic familiarity than from linguistic form. More broadly, our approach provides a diagnostic for auditing and training LLMs to preserve coherent truth assignments under semantic uncertainty, rather than optimizing for output accuracy alone.

papers.title: Blackbox meets blackbox: Representational Similarity and Stability Analysis of Neural Language Models and Brains
papers.research_question: How sensitive are neural language model representations to prior context, and how do these representations compare to human brain activations during story reading?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Representational Stability Analysis (ReStA) to analyze context-dependence in neural language models, finding that LSTM-based models are more similar to brain representations than transformer-based models, and that deeper layers are more context-dependent.
papers.conclusion: ReStA and RSA are useful for comparing models and brains, but caution is required due to low correlations. LSTM-based models are more similar to brain data, and brain data may only reflect shallow linguistic processing.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM-based models (GoogleLM and ELMO) show higher similarity between their two layers compared to BERT.
For LSTM-based models, the first layer is less sensitive to context length than the last layer, suggesting a hierarchical encoding mechanism.
Transformer-based models (BERT) are more sensitive to context length overall, and their first layer is more context-dependent than the last layer.
Among the models, UniSentEnc learns very different representations from the others, possibly due to different training objectives.
LSTM-based models achieve higher similarity with brain data compared to GloVe and transformer-based models, and their lower layers align better with brain representations.
papers.limitation:
Standard RSA assumes all features of the representational spaces have equal contributions, leading to information loss.
The representational similarity between all models and the brain images remains very low.
Inherent issues in the brain data (e.g., hemodynamic response delay, noise) and complexity of the story reading task make evaluation hard.
future_direction: Perform further analysis on various (bigger) datasets to better interpret what is happening in both the brain and computational models.
Postpone further analysis with the predictive approach (linear regression) to future studies.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we define and apply representational stability analysis (ReStA), an intuitive way of analyzing neural language models. ReStA is a variant of the popular representational similarity analysis (RSA) in cognitive neuroscience. While RSA can be used to compare representations in models, model components, and human brains, ReStA compares instances of the same model, while systematically varying single model parameter. Using ReStA, we study four recent and successful neural language models, and evaluate how sensitive their internal representations are to the amount of prior context. Using RSA, we perform a systematic study of how similar the representational spaces in the first and second (or higher) layers of these models are to each other and to patterns of activation in the human brain. Our results reveal surprisingly strong differences between language models, and give insights into where the deep linguistic processing, that integrates information over multiple sentences, is happening in these models. The combination of ReStA and RSA on models and brains allows us to start addressing the important question of what kind of linguistic processes we can hope to observe in fMRI brain imaging data. In particular, our results suggest that the data on story reading from Wehbe et al. (2014) contains a signal of shallow linguistic processing, but show no evidence on the more interesting deep linguistic processing.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: Birds have four legs?! NumerSense: Probing Numerical Commonsense Knowledge of Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: Does and to what extent do pre-trained language models capture numerical commonsense knowledge, and how robust is this knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a probing task and dataset (NumerSense) to evaluate numerical commonsense knowledge in pre-trained language models, finding that models perform poorly and are brittle to adversarial perturbations.
papers.conclusion: Powerful pre-trained models such as BERT and RoBERTa perform surprisingly poorly on numerical commonsense knowledge even after fine-tuning, and the introduced dataset provides a basis for future improvement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT and RoBERTa perform poorly on numerical commonsense knowledge without fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning with distant supervision improves performance but still far from human performance.
Models are brittle to adversarial examples (e.g., inserting adjectives).
Attention analysis shows that important words for numerical commonsense (subject/object) receive low attention weights.
Open-domain QA models also perform poorly on 'how-many' questions derived from NumerSense.
future_direction: Improving PTLMs' abilities to faithfully capture (numerical) commonsense.
Populating numerical facts in current commonsense knowledge bases.
Improving open-domain QA for 'how-many' questions.
Incorporating more structured inductive biases (e.g., dependencies and semantic roles) in pre-training.
Controlling bias in masked language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recent works show that pre-trained language models (PTLMs), such as BERT, possess certain commonsense and factual knowledge. They suggest that it is promising to use PTLMs as "neural knowledge bases" via predicting masked words. Surprisingly, we find that this may not work for numerical commonsense knowledge (e.g., a bird usually has two legs). In this paper, we investigate whether and to what extent we can induce numerical commonsense knowledge from PTLMs as well as the robustness of this process. To study this, we introduce a novel probing task with a diagnostic dataset, NumerSense, containing 13.6k masked-word-prediction probes (10.5k for fine-tuning and 3.1k for testing). Our analysis reveals that: (1) BERT and its stronger variant RoBERTa perform poorly on the diagnostic dataset prior to any fine-tuning; (2) fine-tuning with distant supervision brings some improvement; (3) the best supervised model still performs poorly as compared to human performance (54.06% vs 96.3% in accuracy).

papers.title: The LLM Language Network: A Neuroscientific Approach for Identifying Causally Task-Relevant Units
papers.research_question: Does specialization for language (and other cognitive domains) emerge in large language models, and what is the causal role of such specialized units?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired method to identify language-selective units in LLMs and demonstrates their causal role in language processing through ablation studies.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop specialized language units that are causally important for language processing, similar to the human brain, but specialization for other cognitive domains is less consistent.
papers.key_findings:
Language-selective units can be identified in LLMs using the same functional localization method as in neuroscience.
Ablating even a small percentage (e.g., 1%) of language-selective units causes significant performance drops in language tasks, while ablating random units does not.
The language-selective units in LLMs show similar response profiles to the human language network (e.g., stronger responses to sentences than to non-words, arithmetic, or code).
The language-selective units are more aligned to brain recordings from the human language network than random units, especially when selecting a small subset of units.
Specialization for other cognitive domains (reasoning and theory of mind) is not consistently found across LLMs, with only a subset of models showing such specialization.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focused on models smaller than 13 billion parameters, which may not capture specialization in larger models.
They evaluated Theory of Mind and Multiple Demand units using only one benchmark each (TOMi for ToM and MATH for MD), which may not be comprehensive.
The localizers are adapted from neuroscience and may be constrained by the stimuli sets traditionally used in neuroscience.
future_direction: Expanding the study to include more models and a broader set of benchmarks.
Developing more targeted and robust localizers not restricted by neuroscience stimuli.
Analyzing varying numbers of selective units for MD and ToM networks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities on not just language tasks, but also various tasks that are not linguistic in nature, such as logical reasoning and social inference. In the human brain, neuroscience has identified a core language system that selectively and causally supports language processing. We here ask whether similar specialization for language emerges in LLMs. We identify language-selective units within 18 popular LLMs, using the same localization approach that is used in neuroscience. We then establish the causal role of these units by demonstrating that ablating LLM language-selective units -- but not random units -- leads to drastic deficits in language tasks. Correspondingly, language-selective LLM units are more aligned to brain recordings from the human language system than random units. Finally, we investigate whether our localization method extends to other cognitive domains: while we find specialized networks in some LLMs for reasoning and social capabilities, there are substantial differences among models. These findings provide functional and causal evidence for specialization in large language models, and highlight parallels with the functional organization in the brain.

papers.title: Attention Satisfies: A Constraint-Satisfaction Lens on Factual Errors of Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) internally behave when they generate factually incorrect text, and can attention to constraint tokens predict factual errors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds a strong positive relationship between an LLM's attention to constraint tokens and the factual accuracy of its generations. It proposes SAT Probe, a method that probes attention patterns to predict factual errors and constraint satisfaction.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that attention patterns in LLMs provide a reliable signal for predicting factual errors, contributing to the mechanistic understanding of LLMs and offering a pathway to enhance their reliability.
papers.key_findings:
Attention to constraint tokens strongly correlates with the factual correctness of LLM generations.
SAT Probe, a linear probe on attention weights, can predict factual errors comparably to the model's own confidence score.
Larger LLMs tend to pay more attention to constraint tokens and achieve higher factual accuracy.
The total attention contribution from constraints across layers can be used to predict LLM success on factual queries.
Attention patterns can be used for early error identification, potentially stopping costly generation early.
papers.limitation: Exact match is used as a strict verification criterion for single-constraint queries, which could introduce noise to evaluations.
papers.abstract: We investigate the internal behavior of Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) when they generate factually incorrect text. We propose modeling factual queries as constraint satisfaction problems and use this framework to investigate how the LLM interacts internally with factual constraints. We find a strong positive relationship between the LLM's attention to constraint tokens and the factual accuracy of generations. We curate a suite of 10 datasets containing over 40,000 prompts to study the task of predicting factual errors with the Llama-2 family across all scales (7B, 13B, 70B). We propose SAT Probe, a method probing attention patterns, that can predict factual errors and fine-grained constraint satisfaction, and allow early error identification. The approach and findings take another step towards using the mechanistic understanding of LLMs to enhance their reliability.

papers.title: Exploring Multilingual Probing in Large Language Models: A Cross-Language Analysis
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether other languages achieve comparable probing accuracy to English, whether they exhibit similar layer-wise behavioral patterns to English, and what the similarities are between probing vectors across different languages.
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends probing techniques to a multilingual context and reveals significant disparities in LLMs' performance and representational qualities between high-resource and low-resource languages.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight significant disparities in LLMs' multilingual capabilities and suggest that these models may not be learning deeper linguistic concepts effectively across all languages, especially low-resource ones.
papers.key_findings:
High-resource languages achieve higher probing accuracy than low-resource languages.
High-resource languages exhibit similar layer-wise trends to English, with accuracy improving in deeper layers, while low-resource languages show stable or only slight improvement.
Probing vectors of high-resource languages are more similar to each other, while low-resource languages have lower similarities among themselves and with high-resource languages.
papers.limitation:
Using machine translation to generate prompts and questions may introduce noise.
Only five open-source LLMs and two datasets are experimented with, limiting generalizability.
Only linear classifier probing is used; more sophisticated probing methods could offer deeper insights.
future_direction: Develop more equitable and effective multilingual language models that can better capture universal linguistic concepts.
Extend the research to multimodal models that incorporate visual and textual information.
Explore more sophisticated probing methods beyond linear classifiers.
papers.abstract: Probing techniques for large language models (LLMs) have primarily focused on English, overlooking the vast majority of the world's languages. In this paper, we extend these probing methods to a multilingual context, investigating the behaviors of LLMs across diverse languages. We conduct experiments on several open-source LLM models, analyzing probing accuracy, trends across layers, and similarities between probing vectors for multiple languages. Our key findings reveal: (1) a consistent performance gap between high-resource and low-resource languages, with high-resource languages achieving significantly higher probing accuracy; (2) divergent layer-wise accuracy trends, where high-resource languages show substantial improvement in deeper layers similar to English; and (3) higher representational similarities among high-resource languages, with low-resource languages demonstrating lower similarities both among themselves and with high-resource languages. These results highlight significant disparities in LLMs' multilingual capabilities and emphasize the need for improved modeling of low-resource languages.

papers.title: Uncovering Constraint-Based Behavior in Neural Models via Targeted\n Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: Does competition between linguistic constraints obscure underlying linguistic knowledge in language models, and can targeted fine-tuning re-weight constraints to uncover such knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Models need to learn both linguistic constraints and their relative ranking; targeted fine-tuning can re-weight constraints to uncover dormant linguistic knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Mismatches between model and human linguistic behavior arise from either failure to learn constraints or failure to learn their ranking; targeted fine-tuning can help understand and adjust constraint rankings.
papers.key_findings:
English and Chinese models show an implicit causality (IC) bias, but Spanish and Italian models do not, due to competition with the pro-drop constraint.
Targeted fine-tuning demoting pro-drop in Spanish and Italian uncovers underlying IC knowledge.
Targeted fine-tuning promoting pro-drop in English and Chinese diminishes the IC bias.
Models learn linguistic constraints but may rank them incorrectly, leading to non-human-like behavior.
The failure to exhibit human-like behavior can be due to either not learning a constraint or not learning the correct constraint ranking.
future_direction: Pair behavioral analyses with representational probing to link model representations and behavior.
Explore constraint competition in different models like GPT-2.
Investigate other linguistic phenomena and constraints.
papers.abstract:
A growing body of literature has focused on detailing the linguistic
knowledge embedded in large, pretrained language models. Existing work has
shown that non-linguistic biases in models can drive model behavior away from
linguistic generalizations. We hypothesized that competing linguistic processes
within a language, rather than just non-linguistic model biases, could obscure
underlying linguistic knowledge. We tested this claim by exploring a single
phenomenon in four languages: English, Chinese, Spanish, and Italian. While
human behavior has been found to be similar across languages, we find
cross-linguistic variation in model behavior. We show that competing processes
in a language act as constraints on model behavior and demonstrate that
targeted fine-tuning can re-weight the learned constraints, uncovering
otherwise dormant linguistic knowledge in models. Our results suggest that
models need to learn both the linguistic constraints in a language and their
relative ranking, with mismatches in either producing non-human-like behavior.

papers.title: Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
papers.research_question: How is content-independent syllogistic reasoning internalized in LMs during pre-training? Are content-independent mechanisms disentangled from world knowledge and belief biases? Does the core reasoning mechanism generalize across syllogistic schemes, model sizes, and architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a sufficient and necessary circuit for syllogistic reasoning involving middle-term suppression, showing that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms that are susceptible to contamination from world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn transferable reasoning mechanisms but such mechanisms are contaminated and suppressed by the world knowledge acquired during pre-training, indicating a lack of generalizable abstract logical primitives.
papers.key_findings:
The circuit for syllogistic reasoning involves a three-stage mechanism: long induction, duplication, suppression, and mover heads.
The circuit is necessary and sufficient for symbolic syllogistic reasoning.
The circuit transfers to non-symbolic arguments but is contaminated by belief biases, with additional attention heads encoding world knowledge.
The circuit generalizes across unconditionally valid syllogistic schemes where models achieve high accuracy.
The suppression mechanism pattern is compatible across different model families and sizes, though with increasing complexity in larger models.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is confined to specific syllogistic reasoning templates and does not consider more complex scenarios.
The experimentation is confined due to the intricate level of granularity and computational complexity required in circuit analysis.
future_direction: Further studies to understand how the discovered symbolic circuit can be effectively disentangled from world knowledge to enable systematic generalization in LMs’ reasoning.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on reasoning in language models (LMs) have sparked a debate on whether they can learn systematic inferential principles or merely exploit superficial patterns in the training data. To understand and uncover the mechanisms adopted for formal reasoning in LMs, this paper presents a mechanistic interpretation of syllogistic inference. Specifically, we present a methodology for circuit discovery aimed at interpreting content-independent and formal reasoning mechanisms. Through two distinct intervention methods, we uncover a sufficient and necessary circuit involving middle-term suppression that elucidates how LMs transfer information to derive valid conclusions from premises. Furthermore, we investigate how belief biases manifest in syllogistic inference, finding evidence of partial contamination from additional attention heads responsible for encoding commonsense and contextualized knowledge. Finally, we explore the generalization of the discovered mechanisms across various syllogistic schemes, model sizes and architectures. The identified circuit is sufficient and necessary for syllogistic schemes on which the models achieve high accuracy (>60%), with compatible activation patterns across models of different families. Overall, our findings suggest that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms, but that, at the same time, such mechanisms do not involve generalizable and abstract logical primitives, being susceptible to contamination by the same world knowledge acquired during pre-training.

papers.title: Large Reasoning Models Are (Not Yet) Multilingual Latent Reasoners
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve strong performance on mathematical reasoning tasks, often attributed to their capability to generate explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations. However, recent work shows that LRMs often arrive at the correct answer before completing these textual reasoning steps, indicating the presence of latent reasoning -- internal, non-verbal computation encoded in hidden states. While this phenomenon has been explored in English, its multilingual behavior remains largely unknown. In this paper, we conduct a systematic investigation of multilingual latent reasoning in LRMs across 11 languages. Using a truncation-based strategy, we examine how the correct answer emerges as the model is given only partial reasoning traces, allowing us to measure stepwise latent prediction formation. Our results reveal clear evidence of multilingual latent reasoning, though unevenly: strong in resource-rich languages, weaker in low-resource ones, and broadly less observable on harder benchmarks. To understand whether these differences reflect distinct internal mechanisms, we further perform representational analyses. Despite surface-level disparities, we find that the internal evolution of predictions is highly consistent across languages and broadly aligns with English -- a pattern suggesting an English-centered latent reasoning pathway.

papers.title: Causal interventions expose implicit situation models for commonsense language understanding
papers.research_question: How do transformer models construct implicit situation models to guide pronoun resolution in commonsense language understanding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a circuit of attention heads responsible for propagating contextual information in transformer models for pronoun resolution, using causal interventions and controlled datasets.
papers.conclusion: The study provides preliminary evidence for distinct neural pathways underlying implicit situation models in transformer models, highlighting the value of causal interventions for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
A small circuit of attention heads propagates information from context words to guide pronoun resolution.
Syntax-based pronoun resolution uses more localized pathways compared to context-based resolution involving situation models.
Larger models like ALBERT-xxlarge show better performance and more distinct circuits for situation models.
papers.limitation: Single-site interchange interventions may over-count synergies and under-count redundancies in circuits.
future_direction: Explore settings requiring richer interpretations beyond pronoun resolution.
Use chain-of-thought prompting to expose situation models more explicitly in auto-regressive models.
papers.abstract: Accounts of human language processing have long appealed to implicit ``situation models'' that enrich comprehension with relevant but unstated world knowledge. Here, we apply causal intervention techniques to recent transformer models to analyze performance on the Winograd Schema Challenge (WSC), where a single context cue shifts interpretation of an ambiguous pronoun. We identify a relatively small circuit of attention heads that are responsible for propagating information from the context word that guides which of the candidate noun phrases the pronoun ultimately attends to. We then compare how this circuit behaves in a closely matched ``syntactic'' control where the situation model is not strictly necessary. These analyses suggest distinct pathways through which implicit situation models are constructed to guide pronoun resolution.

papers.title: The Vector Grounding Problem
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded in the world, i.e., have intrinsic meaning, despite being trained only on text data without direct interaction with the world?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that large language models can achieve referential grounding (intrinsic meaning) through selection processes in training that endow internal states with representational functions, even without multimodality or embodiment.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can, in principle and in some cases in practice, have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded, thus solving the Vector Grounding Problem and possessing intrinsic meaning independently of human interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Distinguishes referential grounding from other forms (sensorimotor, relational, communicative, epistemic) and argues referential grounding is the only kind essential to solving the Vector Grounding Problem.
Proposes that referential grounding requires two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories: causal-informational relations to the world and a history of selection that endows internal states with the function of carrying this information.
Argues that post-training (e.g., preference tuning for factual accuracy) can establish selection processes that confer world-involving representational functions to LLM internal states.
Suggests that pre-training might, under specific conditions, also lead to world-involving representational functions through implicit extra-linguistic success conditions in the training data.
Contends that in-context learning could, in principle, allow LLMs to acquire world-involving representational functions during inference without parameter updates.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) produce seemingly meaningful outputs, yet they are trained on text alone without direct interaction with the world. This leads to a modern variant of the classical symbol grounding problem in AI: can LLMs' internal states and outputs be about extra-linguistic reality, independently of the meaning human interpreters project onto them? We argue that they can. We first distinguish referential grounding -- the connection between a representation and its worldly referent -- from other forms of grounding and argue it is the only kind essential to solving the problem. We contend that referential grounding is achieved when a system's internal states satisfy two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories of representation: (1) they stand in appropriate causal-informational relations to the world, and (2) they have a history of selection that has endowed them with the function of carrying this information. We argue that LLMs can meet both conditions, even without multimodality or embodiment.

papers.title: Language Conflict in the Bilingual Brain
papers.abstract: The large majority of humankind is more or less fluent in 2 or even more languages. This raises the fundamental question how the language network in the brain is organized such that the correct target language is selected at a particular occasion. Here we present behavioral and functional magnetic resonance imaging data showing that bilingual processing leads to language conflict in the bilingual brain even when the bilinguals' task only required target language knowledge. This finding demonstrates that the bilingual brain cannot avoid language conflict, because words from the target and nontarget languages become automatically activated during reading. Importantly, stimulus-based language conflict was found in brain regions in the LIPC associated with phonological and semantic processing, whereas response-based language conflict was only found in the pre-supplementary motor area/anterior cingulate cortex when language conflict leads to response conflicts.

papers.title: Neural differences in the processing of semantic relationships across cultures
papers.abstract: The current study employed functional MRI to investigate the contribution of domain-general (e.g. executive functions) and domain-specific (e.g. semantic knowledge) processes to differences in semantic judgments across cultures. Previous behavioral experiments have identified cross-cultural differences in categorization, with East Asians preferring strategies involving thematic or functional relationships (e.g. cow-grass) and Americans preferring categorical relationships (e.g. cow-chicken). East Asians and American participants underwent functional imaging while alternating between categorical or thematic strategies to sort triads of words, as well as matching words on control trials. Many similarities were observed. However, across both category and relationship trials compared to match (control) trials, East Asians activated a frontal-parietal network implicated in controlled executive processes, whereas Americans engaged regions of the temporal lobes and the cingulate, possibly in response to conflict in the semantic content of information. The results suggest that cultures differ in the strategies employed to resolve conflict between competing semantic judgments.

papers.title: Distinct distributed patterns of neural activity are associated with two languages in the bilingual brain
papers.abstract: A large body of previous neuroimaging studies suggests that multiple languages are processed and organized in a single neuroanatomical system in the bilingual brain, although differential activation may be seen in some studies because of different proficiency levels and/or age of acquisition of the two languages. However, one important possibility is that the two languages may involve interleaved but functionally independent neural populations within a given cortical region, and thus, distinct patterns of neural computations may be pivotal for the processing of the two languages. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and multivariate pattern analyses, we tested this possibility in Chinese-English bilinguals when they performed an implicit reading task. We found a broad network of regions wherein the two languages evoked different patterns of activity, with only partially overlapping patterns of voxels in a given region. These regions, including the middle occipital cortices, fusiform gyri, and lateral temporal, temporoparietal, and prefrontal cortices, are associated with multiple aspects of language processing. The results suggest the functional independence of neural computations underlying the representations of different languages in bilinguals.

papers.title: Bilingual language processing relies on shared semantic representations that are modulated by each language
papers.abstract: Abstract Billions of people throughout the world are bilingual, and they can extract meaning from multiple languages. While some evidence suggests that there is a shared system in the human brain for processing semantic information from native and non-native languages, other evidence suggests that semantic processing is language-specific. We conducted a study to determine how semantic information for different languages is represented in the brains of bilinguals. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was used to record brain responses while participants read several hours of natural narratives in their native (Chinese) and non-native (English) languages. These data were then used to compare semantic representations between the two languages. We find that semantic representations are largely shared between languages, but that there are fine-grained differences in the representation of some semantic categories across languages. These results reconcile current competing theories of bilingual language processing. Significance Statement Bilinguals understand the meaning of words in multiple languages. Whether this capacity reflects a shared brain system for processing both native and non-native languages, or whether processing is language-specific is still unclear. Here, we examine whether and how semantic representations in the brain support shared and/or language-specific processing. We recorded brain activity from participants reading narratives in their native (Chinese) and non-native (English) languages, and modeled how their brains represent word meaning in each language. We show that semantic representations are similar between the two language conditions, and that these representations are systematically modulated between native and non-native language comprehension.

papers.title: Brain-Based Translation: fMRI Decoding of Spoken Words in Bilinguals Reveals Language-Independent Semantic Representations in Anterior Temporal Lobe
papers.abstract: Bilinguals derive the same semantic concepts from equivalent, but acoustically different, words in their first and second languages. The neural mechanisms underlying the representation of language-independent concepts in the brain remain unclear. Here, we measured fMRI in human bilingual listeners and reveal that response patterns to individual spoken nouns in one language (e.g., "horse" in English) accurately predict the response patterns to equivalent nouns in the other language (e.g., "paard" in Dutch). Stimuli were four monosyllabic words in both languages, all from the category of "animal" nouns. For each word, pronunciations from three different speakers were included, allowing the investigation of speaker-independent representations of individual words. We used multivariate classifiers and a searchlight method to map the informative fMRI response patterns that enable decoding spoken words within languages (within-language discrimination) and across languages (across-language generalization). Response patterns discriminative of spoken words within language were distributed in multiple cortical regions, reflecting the complexity of the neural networks recruited during speech and language processing. Response patterns discriminative of spoken words across language were limited to localized clusters in the left anterior temporal lobe, the left angular gyrus and the posterior bank of the left postcentral gyrus, the right posterior superior temporal sulcus/superior temporal gyrus, the right medial anterior temporal lobe, the right anterior insula, and bilateral occipital cortex. These results corroborate the existence of "hub" regions organizing semantic-conceptual knowledge in abstract form at the fine-grained level of within semantic category discriminations.

papers.title: Individual differences in representational similarity of first and second languages in the bilingual brain
papers.abstract: Current theories of bilingualism disagree on the extent to which separate brain regions are used to maintain or process one's first and second language. The present study took a novel multivariate approach to address this question. We examined whether bilinguals maintain distinct neural representations of two languages; specifically, we tested whether brain areas that are involved in processing word meaning in either language are reliably representing each language differently, and whether language representation is influenced by individual differences in proficiency level and age of acquisition (AoA) of L2. Thirty-one English-Mandarin bilingual adults performed a picture-word matching task in both languages. We then used representational similarity analysis to examine which brain regions reliably showed different patterns of activity for each language. We found that both proficiency and AoA predicted dissimilarity between language representations in several brain areas within the language network as well as several regions of the ventral visual pathway, demonstrating that top-down language knowledge and individual language experience shapes concept representation in this processing stream. The results support the model of an integrated language system in bilinguals, along with a novel description of how representations for each language change with proficiency level and L2 AoA.

papers.title: The neural bases of the bilingual advantage in cognitive control: An investigation of conflict adaptation phenomena.
papers.abstract: The present dissertation examines the effects of bilingualism on cognitive control, the ability to regulate attention, particularly in the face of multiple, competing sources of information. Across four experiments, I assess the conflict monitoring theory of the so-called "bilingual advantage", which states that bilinguals are better than monolinguals at detecting conflict between multiple sources of information and flexibly recruiting cognitive control to resolve such competition. In Experiment 1, I show that conflict adaptation, the phenomenon that individuals get better at resolving conflict immediately after encountering conflict, occurs across domains, a pre-requisite to determining whether bilingualism can improve conflict monitoring on non-linguistic tasks. Experiments 2 and 3 compare behavioral and neural conflict adaptation effects in bilinguals and monolinguals. I find that bilinguals are more accurate at detecting initial conflicts and show corresponding increases in activation in neural regions implicated in language-switching. Finally, Experiment 4 extends the bilingual advantage in conflict monitoring to syntactic ambiguity resolution and recognition memory.

papers.title: Neural basis of bilingual language control
papers.abstract: Acquiring and speaking a second language increases demand on the processes of language control for bilingual as compared to monolingual speakers. Language control for bilingual speakers involves the ability to keep the two languages separated to avoid interference and to select one language or the other in a given conversational context. This ability is what we refer with the term "bilingual language control" (BLC). It is now well established that the architecture of this complex system of language control encompasses brain networks involving cortical and subcortical structures, each responsible for different cognitive processes such as goal maintenance, conflict monitoring, interference suppression, and selective response inhibition. Furthermore, advances have been made in determining the overlap between the BLC and the nonlinguistic executive control networks, under the hypothesis that the BLC processes are just an instantiation of a more domain-general control system. Here, we review the current knowledge about the neural basis of these control systems. Results from brain imaging studies of healthy adults and on the performance of bilingual individuals with brain damage are discussed.

papers.title: Do Bilinguals Access a Shared or Separate Conceptual Store? Creating False Memories in a Mixed-Language Paradigm
papers.abstract: A central focus of bilingualisrn research is the representation of two language systems in memory. The Revised Hierarchical Model (Kroll & Stewart, l994) predicts that bilinguals access conceptual information from both languages simultaneously. To test this hypothesis, the present study attempted to create false memories across languages. Twenty-two Spanish-English bilinguals participated in a mixed language associative list paradigm. False recognition of target words was significantly higher than false recognition of control words, both within and between languages. These results provide evidence for a shared conceptual store and parallel activation of languages, supporting the Revised Hierarchical Model.

papers.title: Neurolinguistics: Structure, Function, and Connectivity in the Bilingual Brain
papers.abstract: Advances in neuroimaging techniques and analytic methods have led to a proliferation of studies investigating the impact of bilingualism on the cognitive and brain systems in humans. Lately, these findings have attracted much interest and debate in the field, leading to a number of recent commentaries and reviews.
